name: HU6

lead: HU6 is an experimental pill from Rivus Pharmaceuticals designed to deliver DNP, a historic fat-burning mitochondrial uncoupler, in a more controlled way. People follow it as a possible safer route to DNP-style fat loss.

After conversion to DNP in the liver, it lets mitochondria lose energy as heat instead of making ATP, so more energy is burned. A 2023 phase 2a trial of 80 people reported reduced liver fat versus placebo over 61 days, and it is in phase 2 trials for fatty liver, obesity and heart failure.

paras: It is available only inside clinical trials, as a once-daily pill. It is not sold as a product.

Flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were most common in the trial. It is unapproved anywhere. DNP itself was judged too toxic for human consumption, has caused fatal overdoses and is banned for human consumption.

angle.text: HU6 is a slow-release prodrug of DNP that uncouples mitochondria so more energy is burned as heat, aiming at fat loss and a leaner look. A 2023 phase 2a trial reported lower liver fat, and it is not available as a product.

lead: HU6 is an investigational once-daily oral drug from Rivus Pharmaceuticals. It is a prodrug of 2,4-dinitrophenol (DNP), a mitochondrial uncoupler, and is designed to give more stable blood concentrations than DNP itself.[1][2]

DNP was used for weight loss in the 1930s but was judged too toxic for human consumption and is associated with fatal overdoses, so HU6 is being developed as a controlled alternative.[2] It has been tested in phase 1 and phase 2 trials in obesity-related liver disease, overweight and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction.[1]

The main published trial is a 2023 phase 2a study in people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and high BMI, which reported reductions in liver fat versus placebo.[1] It is not approved anywhere and is not sold as a product.

paras: The phase 2a trial (NCT04874233) was randomised, double-blind and placebo-controlled at a single US site. It enrolled 80 adults aged 28-65 with BMI 28-45 and at least 8% liver fat by MRI-PDFF, who took HU6 or placebo once daily for 61 days. The primary endpoint was relative change in liver fat.[1][3]

Mean liver fat fell by 26.8% (150 mg), 35.6% (300 mg) and 33.0% (450 mg), versus a 5.4% increase on placebo. No serious treatment-emergent adverse events or deaths were reported. Flushing, diarrhoea and palpitations were the most common events in HU6 groups. Three HU6 participants and two placebo participants stopped for adverse events.[1] The trial was funded by Rivus.[1]

Other registered studies include phase 1 safety and pharmacokinetic trials (NCT04463017, NCT04709913, NCT05433506, NCT06325930, NCT07170189), a phase 2 study in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (NCT05284617), a phase 2 study in NASH (NCT05979779) and a phase 2 MASH study that was recruiting in 2026 (NCT07491458). A phase 2a energy-metabolism study in type 2 diabetes (NCT06104358) was withdrawn.[3][4][5][6][7][8][9][10]
HU6 is metabolised in the liver to DNP, which shuttles protons across the mitochondrial membrane and dissipates the gradient that drives ATP production, releasing energy as heat.[2]

DNP is banned for human consumption by the FDA, is banned by WADA since 2015, and was reclassified in the UK as a regulated poison in October 2023. Wikipedia reports that bodybuilders and people with eating disorders obtain it online, and that at least 50 overdose deaths were reported worldwide between 2010 and 2020.[2] HU6 is a distinct, investigational prodrug and is not the same product.

timeline.event: Phase 2a results published in Lancet Gastroenterology & Hepatology.[1]
